Our ancestors held the <term>Romance of the Rose</term> <note>original: "Roman de la Rose," a celebrated 13th-century allegorical poem that explores the art of love through a dream vision.</note> in such high esteem that it would be a sign of either too much contempt or too marked an ingratitude not to hold it in some regard ourselves. Guillaume de Lorris, who first undertook this romance, was from the small town in Gâtinois <note>A former province of France; the town is modern-day Lorris in the Loiret department.</note> from which he took his name. ### *Jean de Meung continues the Romance.*

Jean de Meung, nicknamed *Clopinel* <note>Derived from an Old French term meaning "the hobbler," a reference to his physical disability.</note> due to a defect he had in one leg, came next and brought this romance to its end—I might even say to its perfection. He possessed more vivacity than Guillaume de Lorris; he was just as good a poet, but he did not possess as much focus on morals <term>mœurs: here referring to the depiction of social character and ethical conduct</term> and sentiment as his predecessor. The beauty of the romance that fell into his hands provided him the opportunity to continue such a fine beginning. He did so with such success that this book, the oracle of our ancestors, is still today enjoyed by people of wit who have the time to read it and the facility to understand it <note>A reference to the fact that by the 18th century, the Middle French of the 13th century was becoming difficult for the general public to read without study.</note>.

It is well known that the order of the Templars <note>The Poor Fellow-Soldiers of Christ and of the Temple of Solomon, a wealthy and powerful Catholic military order.</note> was not abolished until 1309. Several of its members had been arrested as early as the year 1307, accused, it was said, of the most horrible crimes; these rumors, whether true or false, had been circulating for at least a year or two before that. Thus, given the prejudice then prevalent, this order was not something to be cited as a regular body <note>A religious community living under a "rule" (*regula*), such as monks or friars.</note> in which one could work toward their salvation. Yet this is precisely what Jean de Meung does when he says, around line 12132:

> If he entered, according to the precept <gloss>original: "comment" — meaning a precept or scriptural commentary</gloss>
> Of Scripture, into an Abbey

> As are now these white Monks <gloss>The Cistercians of Citeaux, known for their white habits</gloss>,
> These black monks <gloss>The Benedictines of Saint-Benoit, known for their black habits</gloss> and these regular Canons <gloss>The Canons Regular, priests living in community under a rule</gloss>,

->PREFACE. 11<-

This is the most recent historical fact by which one can judge the time when this romance was written. All the other points of modern history scattered throughout this work span from the year 1100 to the time we have just noted. Jean de Meung <note>The second author of the *Romance of the Rose*, who added over 17,000 lines to the original unfinished poem.</note> was young when he wrote this work; he informs us of this himself, in general terms, at the beginning of his *Codicil* <note>A poetic testament or "little code" attributed to Jean de Meung, often included in manuscripts of the Romance.</note>:

> In my youth I composed many a poem¹ out of vanity,
> In which many people have often taken delight.²

And since we find elsewhere that it was just as he was leaving his childhood, we believe it might have been around his 22^e^ year. This is the proper time for creating and practicing romances.

### *The Satire Pervading this Romance.*

Satire rules no less in this romance than love; perhaps it is even more wisely handled here than that passion. At times, it revolves around the faults of the female sex <note>original: "défauts du sexe." Jean de Meun, the author of the second part of the *Romance of the Rose*, was famously criticized by historical figures like Christine de Pizan for his harsh portrayals of women.</note>, which he exaggerates a bit too sharply and in terms for which he has been justly criticized. At other times, he takes aim at the inconsistent behavior shown by lovers before and after their marriage. In another instance, he attacks the licentiousness of the cloisters <term>cloisters: monasteries and convents where monks and nuns lived in religious seclusion</term>, where even chastity was not safe. And dare I say that, while living under royal authority, he even ventures to paint quite a bold picture of the way in which nations first gave themselves kings? After having spoken of the simple and natural life of the first humans, he shows the dissensions and evils brought about by private property and the division of goods. This is what he says at verse 10060:

> And the earth itself they divided,*

Our language was only just emerging from the <term>barbarism</term> <note>In this context, "barbarism" refers to the perceived unrefined or "uncivilized" state of the French language during the Middle Ages compared to the classical standards of the author's own time.</note> left to it by the <term>Celtic</term> <note>Refers to the ancient Gaulish linguistic roots.</note> and <term>Teutonic</term> <note>original: *theudesque*; referring to the early Germanic languages that influenced the development of Old French.</note> languages when this <term>romance</term> <note>original: *roman*; the French term for a long narrative work, specifically the *Romance of the Rose*.</note> was begun. # THE ROMANCE
### OF
## THE ROSE

->Here is the Romance of the Rose,<-
->Where all the Art of Love is enclosed.<-

MANY people say that in dreams
There are nothing but fables and lies;
But one can dream such dreams
Which are not at all lying;
Rather, they are afterwards clearly evident:
I can indeed find a guarantor for this
In an author named <term>Macrobius</term> <note>Macrobius was a 5th-century Latin writer whose commentary on the "Dream of Scipio" was the primary medieval authority on the significance and interpretation of dreams.</note>,
Who does not hold dreams to be <term>deceptions</term> <note>original: "lobes"; meaning trifles, jokes, or deceitful nonsense.</note>,
But instead wrote of the vision
That happened to <term>King Scipio</term> <note>Scipio Africanus the Younger. The "Dream of Scipio" (Somnium Scipionis) originally written by Cicero and commented on by Macrobius, describes a vision of the celestial spheres and the immortality of the soul.</note>.
Whoever thinks or whoever says
That this is a <term>folly</term> <note>original: "musardie"; refers to a state of idling, distraction, or a foolish waste of time.</note>

In one way it anoints me, in another it stings <note>original: "cuyst." Literally "cooks" or "burns." It describes the smarting, searing sensation of the wound.</note> me;

<summary>The narrator experiences the dual nature of love as he is healed by a divine ointment even while the iron tips of six arrows remain lodged in his heart. Surrounded by vermin and filth,
Who has not even a crust of barley or oat bread.
He does not die from his suffering:
**Hope** <note>In the medieval tradition of courtly love, Hope (Esperance) is a personified virtue who sustains the lover in the face of despair, preventing him from giving up.</note> brings him comfort,

### (v. 4241.)

Love releases those who are bound;

True Love, which never ceases;

Loyal Love compels even God; <note>The original text suggests that Love "does force" to God, a medieval theological concept meaning that God’s own nature as Love necessitates His mercy and His bond with humanity.</note>
For Love strives toward loving. <note>original: "d'amer s'efforce." There is a frequent wordplay in Middle French between *amer* (to love) and *amer* (bitter). Here, it emphasizes the intense effort of the soul to remain in a state of devotion.</note>

As long as it is healthy and alive;
Then it sleeps in meditation,

There one feels everything that can be possessed,
There one learns everything that can be learned.

-># THE ROMANCE<-

<meta>(v. 4586.)</meta>

They find no one to <term>succor</term> <note>original: "sequeure." To help or assist in a time of difficulty.</note> them;
But the true friend remains,
Who does not love for the sake of riches—
So full of <term>nobility</term> <note>original: "noblesses." In this context, it refers to a moral excellence or "nobility of heart" rather than inherited social rank.</note> is his heart—
Nor for any profit he expects to gain from it.
Such a one helps and defends them;
For <term>Fortune</term> <note>The goddess Fortuna was believed to control external goods like money and power, but she had no power over internal virtues or true bonds of the soul.</note> has no power over such a thing:
A friend, if he is a true friend, always loves.

If one were to draw a sword against a friend,
Would that not sever the love?
[Yes,] except in these cases I wish to mention:
One can lose a friend through pride, through anger,
Through <term>reproach</term> <note>The act of shaming or severely criticizing a friend for their failings.</note>, and through revealing
Secrets that ought to be kept hidden,
And through the painful wound
Of venomous <term>detraction</term> <note>original: "détraction." The act of slandering or belittling someone's reputation behind their back.</note>.
In such circumstances, friends would flee.

<vocab>Fortune, friend, nobility, slander, Romance of the Rose, Jean de Meun</vocab>

<summary>Reason describes how fair-weather friends mock and abandon those who have lost their wealth, while asserting that true friendship is a noble bond immune to the fluctuations of Fortune, though it can be destroyed by betrayal or slander.</summary>

In this world, no one would be poor,

The willows <note>original: "saulx"</note> which ought to be barren <note>original: "brehains" — sterile or unable to bear fruit.</note>,
There they bloom and receive fruit;
Against the vine the elm tree strives,
And takes from it the shape of the grape <note>In agricultural tradition, vines were often grown up elm trees (the "marriage" of the vine and elm). Here, the elm unnaturally usurps the vine's identity.</note>.
The nightingale sings there but rarely;
But there brays and laments loudly
The owl <note>original: "chahuen" — a screech owl or long-eared owl, traditionally a bird of ill-omen.</note> with its great shaggy head <note>original: "hure" — a term used for the bristly head of a wild boar, suggesting the owl's frightening appearance.</note>,
Prophet of misfortune <note>original: "male adventure"</note>,
Hideous messenger of sorrow,
In its voice, in form and in color.
Through there, whether it be summer or winter,
Two different rivers run together,
Springing from different fountains
Which come from different veins;
One yields waters so sweet <note>original: "doulcereuses"</note>,
So savory, so honeyed,
That there is no one who does not drink of it—
Indeed, much more than he ought,
If he can quench his thirst there,
So sweet and precious is this drink;

<summary>Reason describes the perversion of nature on Fortune's island, where barren trees bear fruit and symbols of peace wither, while a sweet, addictive river tempts travelers. This represents the deceptive and unpredictable allure of worldly success.</summary>

There is a common saying that is very foolish,

# (v. 7098.) THE ROMANCE

When he knows how to reflect well,
He will not find himself in his greatest ease
Without something that displeases him;
Nor will he ever have so much misfortune,
When he knows how to reflect well,
That he does not find in his discomfort
Something that comforts him,
Whether it be a thing already done or something yet to come,
If he thought well on his situation—
Unless he falls into <term>despair</term> <note>original: *desesperance* — In a medieval context, despair (wanhope) was considered a grave sin because it represented a total loss of faith in God’s mercy.</note>,
Which hinders all sinners,
And for which no one can offer a remedy,
So deeply have I read in the texts <note>original: *la lettre* — Lady Reason refers to the authority of written philosophy and scripture, specifically echoing Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*.</note>.
What use is it then to be angry,
To weep and to grumble?
Rather, take heart and step forward
To receive with patience
Everything that <term>Fortune</term> gives you,
Whether it be fair or ugly, or evil or good.
Of Fortune the fickle <note>original: *semilleuse* — From the Latin *simulare*; it implies someone who is shifty, deceptive, or puts on a false front.</note>,
And of her perilous wheel <note>The *Rota Fortunae* (Wheel of Fortune) was the most famous medieval metaphor for the randomness of life; the goddess turns the wheel, meaning those who are high today will be low tomorrow.</note>,
I could not count all the turns:
It is the game of "purse in the strap," <note>original: *bourse en courroye* — A medieval swindling game, similar to "fast and loose," where a player tries to catch a loop in a leather strap with a pin or purse, but the dealer always ensures they lose. It signifies that Fortune’s favors are a rigged game.</note>

<summary>Lady Reason advises the Lover that no human experience is purely good or evil, and that the only true defense against the "rigged game" of Fortune is patience and intellectual reflection.</summary>

**Socrates**, however rich he may have been,
Nor do I wish to hear more talk of him.
To my master <note>The God of Love, to whom the Lover swore an oath of fealty earlier in the poem.</note> I wish to go;
I wish to keep my covenant <term>covenant</term> <note>original: *convenant* — a formal, binding agreement or oath of loyalty in the feudal tradition.</note> with him,
For it is right and fitting:
Even if he were to lead me to hell,
I cannot restrain my heart from it;
My heart is no longer my own.
Never yet have I broken it,
Nor do I intend to break
My testament <note>original: *testament* — the Lover views his commitment as a final, legal will or sacred legacy.</note> for the sake of loving another:
To **Fair-Welcome** <note>original: *Bel-Acueil* — a personification representing the receptive and kind aspect of the lady being wooed.</note> I have left it all;
For I know my legacy <term>legacy</term> <note>original: *lais* — a legal term for a bequest; also a pun on a type of narrative poem.</note> well by heart,
And I listen with great impatience
To a confession without repentance <note>The Lover views Reason’s long lecture as a sort of religious "confession" she is forcing upon him, but he refuses to feel the "repentance" required to change his ways.</note>:
Thus I would not [give up] the **Rose**

<summary>The Lover explicitly rejects Lady Reason's advice, dismissing the example of Socrates and reaffirming his absolute feudal loyalty to the God of Love. He declares that his heart is no longer his own and has been entirely bequeathed to Fair-Welcome.</summary>
